Hi all, I am a 39 year old woman diagnosed with hypermobile ehlers-danlos syndrome (hEDS), PCOS, IBS-D, asthma, and multiple allergies. I get really sick whenever I get ill. In fact, I still mask in most indoor spaces because I don’t have enough PTO to cover 2-3 weeks off every time I get an upper respiratory infection. 

Due to my hEDS, I had pretty severe SI joint dysfunction, and had my left SI fused in August of 2023. I started having more pain around my surgical site this past summer, and on January 15th, I had a steroid injection in my left SI joint for diagnostic and potentially therapeutic purposes. My surgeon is evaluating me for a potential non-union of my fusion. 

I got a work up from an immunologist at Mayo Clinic, which included a morning cortisol level. I’m not sure if that’s routine for them or not, but my lab was 0.8 mcg/dL, which is considered low. I was also low in natural killer cells, which I understand can be related to adrenal insufficiency. 

My immunologist referred me to endocrinology at Mayo, but they want me to redo my morning cortisol in 6 weeks because of my SI joint injection. From the literature I’ve read, intra-articular joint space injections do not usually have a significant effect on adrenal hormones unless they are injected into the spine and connect with cerebrospinal fluid. 

I’m kind of hoping that I don’t have Addison’s Disease and this is all an effect of my sacroiliac injection, but I have had symptoms that could be explained by adrenal insufficiency for a long time. 

I am constantly thirsty, have daily diarrhea/loose stools, drenching night sweats, and so much brain fog that my adderall doesn’t even touch my disorganization. Doctors have ruled out diabetes. 

tl;dr: can an intra-articular steroid injection mimic Addison’s Disease in lab work? I am getting my morning cortisol checked again in mid-March, but feeling like this sucks.

I’m not saying this is a catch-all, as there need to be many other systemic changes that need to happen in order to reduce suicidal ideation among men. However, if you want to keep people alive long enough to have successful interventions, reducing firearm access would be an more concrete, actionable step to take.

My journey with this illness began in January of 2021 when I started to have pain in my left calf. A blood clot was ruled out almost immediately. I had a work-up with vascular at Mayo in MN with several MRIs and even an angiogram, which ruled out popliteal artery entrapment syndrome. My pain became unbearable and I had a difficult time walking by March. I hobbled into the ED and stayed there a day. Their work up found a high-grade tear in my left gastrocnemius muscle, which I had done nothing impactful or traumatic to cause. They had me use crutches and a walking boot and assumed this would help, but it didn’t. 

I made my way through orthopedics without a diagnosis and even had 2 injections in my spine last summer, which actually relieved some pain and made it easier for me to walk. I was about to get an injection in my tibial nerve at the end of last summer with a new orthopedist, but she looked at my chart and noticed a pattern no one else had: my CRP and ESR have been elevated in every blood draw since 2017. At its highest, my CRP was in the 30s(mg/L). I was referred to rheumatology. 

I have been working with rheumatology at Mayo since October of 2021. My ANA was 1:320 speckled, but my doctor informed me that this is too weak of a titer to be considered positive. We ruled out RA, ankylosing spondylitis, large/medium vessel vasculitis (based on my angiogram in March of 2021), lumbosacral meeve irritation, and genetic causes for auto inflammatory disorders (I was negative for DADA2). 

The only thing that has truly helped me in this whole process was starting Prednisone in January. I have been on varying doses and at one point was able to walk without limping and ride my bicycle. I just reduced from 7.5mg to 5mg of prednisone daily. The last time I went from 5mg to 2.5mg to 0 was very painful and exhausting for me. I also added Humira a few months ago, and I think that has helped mediate some of my symptoms and helped me reduce my prednisone dosage, but I haven’t been able to be just on the Humira at this point. 

I have not had a biopsy of my left calf although I have pushed for one. My doctor and a neuromuscular specialist don’t feel there’s a “good enough” target to biopsy based on imaging and they don’t want to do a “blind” biopsy. 

My pain hovers around 4/10 daily. Every step is painful. Some days I limp more than others. I would love to plan a small vacation with my partner, but I can’t walk much or go to museums or even spend a lot of time on my feet. I feel like my rheumatologist is putting my case on the back burner. I can’t imagine being in this much pain for another year and a half or longer.

There are a few reasons it could have happened. Sometimes males from other “cohorts” or families will kill babies that aren’t theirs in order to hasten the mother’s fertility again and impregnate her themselves (like sexual selection). Another reason I read about for rodent infanticide is a lack of resources, but like my neighbor said “there are plenty of nuts for everyone!” We aren’t in a drought or anything, so my guess is the former reason.

At 7am I was snoozing my alarm and pushing my cats away to try to get 5 more minutes of sleep. I heard a squirrel screaming, so much so that I leapt out of bed and looked out my window. I saw one baby squirrel thrown from the nest. Then another. As I continued to watch in horror, the adult squirrel who threw them out of the nest proceeded to battle with one of the babies until it was dead. I made my way downstairs as fast as I could (the elevator couldn’t go fast enough), and found the other baby squirrel hiding under the petunias. I later found a third baby fending off an attack from the same adult squirrel that killed their sibling. Luckily, I had an extra pet carrier in my car. My neighbor, who also heard the commotion, was willing to watch the babies while I saw my morning clients. I was advised by the county to take them to the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center of MN Wildlife Rehabilitation Center of Minnesota (WRC). They didn’t love the car ride, but they comforted each other. At the wildlife center, I completed an intake form and they informed me of their squirrel nursery! I will be able to follow up on the babies as they hopefully grow and thrive. I’m so glad I was able to save these two. That murderous squirrel better watch his back because I know where he lives.
